# How a Compiler Transforms a Program into Machine Instructions

A compiler is best understood as a pipeline of transformations, each of which takes a representation of the program at one level of abstraction and produces a representation at a lower or more refined level. The overall journey begins with raw source text—characters typed by a programmer—and ends with machine instructions that a particular processor can execute. Along the way, the compiler must discover the structure of the program, verify that it is meaningful and well-typed, translate it into forms that are convenient for analysis and optimization, improve those forms where possible, and finally emit concrete instructions for a specific target architecture. The stages are not entirely independent; information gathered early (such as symbol tables and type information) is carried forward and used later, and later stages may feed back into earlier ones (for example, optimization may require re-analysis of data flow). Nevertheless, it is useful to describe the pipeline in order: lexical analysis, parsing, type checking, intermediate representation, optimization, and code generation.
